Senses.Explanation: Records use this phrase for words or actions that stop proliferating routes of discrimination and response. The image is “cut off all streams,” and Yunmen-house discussions place it among three phrase-functions alongside covering heaven and earth and following wave after wave. Yuanwu Keqin calls it a solitary voicing of the hidden pivot that cuts off all streams without constraint or turning back. In the Blue Cliff Record he explains that an ordinary Yunmen phrase must contain three phrases: one that covers heaven and earth, one that follows the waves, and one that cuts off all streams. Ruibai Mingxue says that in a single shout the cutting-off phrase sweeps away ordinary and sage and ends conceptual interpretation. Hanyue Fazang describes unconstrained movement as lion-like and stream-cutting, while Feiyin Tongrong pairs the image with a sword across the sky and an iron pillar. Shiyu Mingfang applies it to the power of a fragrant elephant crossing beyond the mind-ocean. Tianyin Yuanxiu nevertheless says that even cutting off all streams remains outside the gate, preventing the phrase from becoming a final attainment-label.

Senses.Explanation: To cut off the tangled vines is the records' recurring closure formula for ending the present chain of explanation, questioning, or verbal entanglement. Huanyou Chuan ends an account when tea arrives with 'cut off the tangled vines and drink tea.' Tianyin Xiu shouts the phrase after extended exhortation and, in another interview, draws once with his staff before saying it. Dahui Zonggao places it at the end of a written exposition whose paper has run out. Guxue Zhenzhe joins cutting the vines to overturning a nest of fixed formulations, while a later hall speaker makes the phrase itself the subject of a public question.

Senses.Explanation: Not yet; not there yet: in the Chan corpus this is especially frequent as a teaching-seat verdict on a reply, shout, verse, or claimed understanding. The exact words (未在) also retain their ordinary temporal force. Zhaozhou Congshen says, 'Not there yet; say more' (未在更道). Gufeng Xiu tells Wanshan Zhengning, 'You have got it, but you are still not there yet' (你也得，只是未在). Fushi Tongxian likewise says, 'Not there yet; say more,' while Tianyin Yuanxiu uses the phrase to reject an attempted deception. Guangxiao Huijue says, 'Even if you reached a thousand years, you still would not yet be old' (直至千歲也未在). Thus the corpus deploys one phrase both as an evaluative reply and in ordinary statements of something not yet reached or completed.
